title: The Library Display
paragraphs: A student reading club was preparing a display for the town library. Its members collected accounts from notebooks, interviews, and short stories. They wanted visitors to notice how a small detail could change the way an event was understood.
The first section of the collection placed these observations side by side. The signs warn hikers about falling rocks.

The class finished by comparing its first impressions with its later interpretations. Some ideas had survived closer examination; others needed to be revised. The students kept the original details visible so that future readers could judge for themselves. They understood that a convincing explanation should connect the evidence clearly while leaving room for questions the records could not answer.

A reader can continue the investigation by choosing one detail and explaining why it matters. The strongest answer will distinguish observation from assumption, consider the circumstances, and identify a question that would require more evidence before it could be answered confidently.

targets.definition: to tell someone of possible danger
